sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Operators across the board agree the vehicle is the business: whatever you park in the driveway decides which manifests you can accept. RouteGenie frames the minivan as the workhorse, citing Indiana Medicaid data where 63.5% of trip requests are ambulatory and 30.3% are wheelchair, which is why a wheelchair-accessible minivan can complete up to 90% of all contracts and is the minimum recommended platform for scaling with brokers [Lh999r_-mi0 @ 00:05:17]. Nemt University's host maps a six-month path from personal car to wheelchair van and is blunt that adding a wheelchair accessible vehicle on top of ambulatory ramps up revenue and is essential if you want to scale [VGWUx-p8MbM @ 00:12:56]. The Wheelchair & Stretcher Transportation Services operator pushes the logic to the ceiling: a Ford Transit fits a stretcher, two wheelchairs, and one ambulatory passenger in one vehicle, and running Caravans on broker work alone is not how you scale [svdIU5f-6tA @ 00:00:39]. NEMT Growth Machine bought into the same thesis with real money, choosing a van with full ambulatory and wheelchair capability because the owners wanted to shoot for as much revenue as possible [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:07:35]. The shared rule: buy capability that matches the highest-value trips in your market.

The second consensus point is that cramped wheelchair vans quietly bleed trips. Jasmine and Monica of MJ Business Academy, five years in business in California, report that rehabilitation-center patients often ride with leg extenders, and a smaller wheelchair van like the ProMaster City cannot fit them, so that trip gets turned away; the same tight cabin blocks multi-loading and blocks hauling a husband and wife who are both in wheelchairs [P_pN6quM3G4 @ 00:03:02]. On a live ride-along they watched a competitor load a reclining wheelchair and called it proof that full cut vans are the best, since a typical side entry van likely could not accommodate that client [ohTDpW0zUS8 @ 00:06:54]. Their own full cut Dodge Caravan carries two ambulatory riders plus one wheelchair with the seats out, or two wheelchairs with the fold-away chairs collapsed [rIDRpTROLM8 @ 00:00:23]. They also flag a regulatory trap that reinforces the same choice: California has been denying rear entry vehicles, and one of their clients with a rear entry wheelchair van was approved by Medicaid only for ambulatory trips because the van lacked an emergency exit, even with a side door [P_pN6quM3G4 @ 00:11:02]. Size, layout, and exit configuration decide your book before marketing ever does.

Baseline equipment is equally settled. RouteGenie lists the non-negotiables as airbags, seat belts, ABS brakes, maintained lights, brakes, and tires, a first aid kit, a fire extinguisher, and GPS tracking, with accessible units needing a 56-inch door opening, ramps or lifts, gear shift interlock, and four tie-downs with lap and shoulder belts; some states bar vehicles older than 15 years from manufacture, and the most common age range cited is 5 to 10 years [Lh999r_-mi0 @ 00:01:26]. MJ Business Academy adds that the fire extinguisher must be mounted inside the van and that a carpet-free floor is a plus because clients have accidents and bodily fluids have to be cleaned fast [rIDRpTROLM8 @ 00:01:54]. NEMT Growth Machine carries disposable gloves, N95 masks, a first aid kit, and a bloodborne pathogen and bodily fluid spill kit in a duffel in the back [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:04:26]. On the human side, RouteGenie's driver profile demands a valid state-issued license, the ability to operate a wheelchair lift, sometimes lifting 50 pounds or more, and training in HIPAA, CPR, and first aid, because this is not taxi or Uber work [qiZqLls0G-E @ 00:00:50]. Skip any of these and the van is not ready to run a manifest.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: NEMT Growth Machine published the cleanest unit economics. Their 2025 Ford Transit 350 XL with a rear loading wheelchair lift cost $87,900 after taxes from Mobility Works in Charlotte, with a warranty; they put $6,000 down and financed the rest at roughly $1,600 a month [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:00:00]. Commercial insurance runs about $17,315 a year, or roughly $1,440 a month, pushing fixed cost above $3,000 a month before oil changes, tire rotations, or gas; they offset fuel by charging for mileage, and they peg the all-in annual figure at about $43,000, or around $45,000 once gas and surprise repairs land [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:00:20]. RouteGenie's 2026 price sheet, built on 2019 used units under 100,000 miles, gives the cheaper on-ramps: a used Grand Caravan runs $13,000 to $16,000, a used Toyota Sienna $21,000 to $24,000, and a used Ford Transit $25,000 to $30,000, against $50,500 new [uJV2f3MOJbI @ 00:01:06]. Nemt University tells beginners to set a hard budget first, whether $7,500, $10,000, or $20,000, then pick cash, financing, or a lease, paying cash if you can so there is no note, and financing only with decent credit and room to cover the payment plus insurance [VGWUx-p8MbM @ 00:04:37].

Inside the box, the mechanics are physical and repeatable. NEMT Growth Machine runs a floor track system: pull a lever and the seats slide to any layout, so a wheelchair rider and caregiver can sit together; every wheelchair gets four track locks, two front and two back, that hook the chair, then two lap belts join in the middle and a shoulder belt completes a full seat belt [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:01:44]. Their add-on list is cheap: a roughly $30 windshield phone mount so drivers stay hands-free, a dash cam plus interior camera at about $180 to $200 that records whenever the van is on, Clorox wipes for every high-touch surface after each rider, an umbrella for door-to-door pickups in the rain, a jack and spare, and three reflective triangles set roughly 10, 100, and 200 feet behind a breakdown [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:02:40]. MJ Business Academy slides a TJ Maxx or Home Goods storage bin into the limited storage area for driver lunches and equipment [rIDRpTROLM8 @ 00:02:16]. For stretcher work, AMS Vans installs a gurney with a quick release lock in a rear entry long channel: lower the gurney all the way, roll the front casters into the antler cradle, and pin it; unbolt the floor mount with a 9/16 ratchet to flip the van back to wheelchair service [-DCWDiGaTn0 @ 00:01:02].

Daily execution starts before dawn. RouteGenie's driver routine begins as early as 4 or 5 a.m. to hit pre-procedure hospital arrivals: clock in through the NEMT app, check fuel, oil, tire pressure, brakes, lights, wheelchair lifts, and securement straps, then run surgery, dialysis, and physical therapy pickups across an 8 to 12 hour shift that closes with a final inspection logged in the app [qiZqLls0G-E @ 00:03:06]. Wait time is billable leverage: on a ride-along, Jasmine and Monica's private client had a 10:30 pickup and had agreed that if the client was not outside at 10:30 the clock starts and wait time gets charged, and they pulled the client's number from the app to call directly [ohTDpW0zUS8 @ 00:05:59]. Cancellations are the bleed. LearnCargo says nine times out of 10 you discover a cancellation on your own at the last minute, sometimes after the broker failed to notify you; the fix is to call the broker and get a note on the client account after a wasted 30-mile run [MOdO2Zzw1wI @ 00:01:02]. RouteGenie's fee model uses a 24-hour free cancellation window, with an example of a $25 fee on a $100 trip canceled inside 24 hours, backed by a written, consistently enforced no-show policy [d8ocN3ERJag @ 00:04:22].

callout.title: Street-Level Moves From Operators Running Vans Daily
callout.body: Small purchasing and operating habits that keep trips on the board, keep the van flexible, and keep wasted miles on the record.
items: Lean on a sharp dealership rep: Jasmine and Monica were set on a smaller van with a bench seat until a Mobility Works rep showed them the extended cut and warned they would limit themselves [MJ Business Academy — P_pN6quM3G4 @ 00:10:25].

Treat a suspiciously cheap Grand Caravan as a red flag, because it was sold exclusively as a fleet vehicle in its final years and extremely low prices might signal poor condition [RouteGenie — uJV2f3MOJbI @ 00:03:21].

Keep the stretcher setup removable: the AMS Vans floor mount sits on two threaded inserts, so a 9/16 ratchet pulls it out and the van runs as a wheelchair accessible unit [AMS Vans — -DCWDiGaTn0 @ 00:01:20].
Train riders to call the broker directly when canceling, and when a broker fails to notify you, call and get a note placed on that client account [LearnCargo — MOdO2Zzw1wI @ 00:00:32].

sop_steps.title: Run Local Market Research and Lock a Budget
sop_steps.action: Research your county broker rules, insurance quotes, vehicle prices, and application fees, then set a hard purchase budget.
sop_steps.detail: Market rules differ by city and county, with some counties requiring a broker for Medicaid work [Nemt University — irqJHXZq5K8 @ 00:04:21]; set a number such as $7,500, $10,000, or $20,000 and choose cash, financing, or lease [Nemt University — VGWUx-p8MbM @ 00:04:37].

sop_steps.title: Buy the Cut and Configuration Your State Will Approve
sop_steps.action: Test extended or full cut vans at a mobility dealer and confirm your state accepts the entry and exit layout.
sop_steps.detail: Smaller vans cannot fit leg extenders or two wheelchairs, and California denied a rear entry wheelchair van for lacking an emergency exit [MJ Business Academy — P_pN6quM3G4 @ 00:11:02].

sop_steps.title: Load Out the Van Kit
sop_steps.action: Install the phone mount, dash and interior cameras, spill kit, gloves, masks, first aid kit, fire extinguisher, triangles, spare, and brochures.
sop_steps.detail: NEMT Growth Machine keeps gloves, N95 masks, a first aid kit, and a bloodborne pathogen spill kit in a rear duffel plus business cards for networking at facilities [NEMT Growth Machine — nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:04:26].

sop_steps.title: Run the Daily Trip Cycle
sop_steps.action: Clock in, complete the pre-trip inspection, send automated reminders, enforce wait time and cancellation policy, and log end-of-shift issues.
sop_steps.detail: Pre-trip checks cover fluids, tires, brakes, lights, lifts, and straps [RouteGenie — qiZqLls0G-E @ 00:03:23]; reminder calls go out the day prior, the morning of, and when the driver is en route [RouteGenie — R4q_XZ1pARQ @ 00:04:11].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over the first vehicle. Nemt University argues ambulatory is the easiest door into the business because a driver who already owns a newer sedan, such as a 2017-era Buick, skips the purchase or lease expense entirely. The host started with one vehicle and a small square magnet on the door, and tells operators not to wait for four or five new trucks [irqJHXZq5K8 @ 00:03:06] [irqJHXZq5K8 @ 00:05:18]. Wheelchair & Stretcher Transportation Services takes the opposite line: stop buying rear entry wheelchair vans, stop letting people say you can start with that, and start with the best. The speaker recommends a Ford Transit, calls it actually cheaper than a Caravan, and says it can carry a stretcher, two wheelchairs, and one ambulatory passenger in one run [svdIU5f-6tA @ 00:00:23]. NEMT Growth Machine sits on the expensive end by choice. The owners bought an $87,900 Ford Transit 350 XL because they wanted to shoot for as much revenue as possible and run anything and everything. They also admit a sedan could be even cheaper for someone who does not want to deal with wheelchairs [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:07:23]. The operator choice comes down to whether cash on hand buys capacity now or the fleet scales later from a personal car.

Entry style and cut length produce a second fault line. Nemt University says its own fleet runs rear entry vehicles, while conceding that a rear ramp carries a slight degree of tilt compared with a side ramp. The host frames the choice as whatever accommodations the operator wants to offer, and points buyers toward pricing a used minivan wheelchair vehicle first [VGWUx-p8MbM @ 00:03:24]. MJ Business Academy pushes the conversation toward cut size rather than door position. Jasmine and Monica say full cut vans are the best after watching another provider load a reclining wheelchair that a side entry van likely could not accommodate [ohTDpW0zUS8 @ 00:06:54]. Their own full cut Dodge Caravan takes two ambulatory riders and one wheelchair with the seats out, or two wheelchairs once the folding seats collapse [rIDRpTROLM8 @ 00:00:23]. They also report California refusing rear entry vans that lack an emergency exit. That left one client with a wheelchair van that was approved only for ambulatory Medicaid trips [P_pN6quM3G4 @ 00:11:02]. The live split is whether a full cut minivan with folding seats is the scalable workhorse, or whether door position and state exit rules decide the purchase before cut length ever matters to the buyer.

Even the money math splits, sometimes inside the same channel. In its ambulatory-versus-wheelchair breakdown, Nemt University says ambulatory is the way to go to maximize what you make, especially on private pay trips where the operator dictates the rate [irqJHXZq5K8 @ 00:03:25]. Yet in its wheelchair van guide, the same host says wheelchair accessible vehicles make more money because the operator is offering more services, and calls an ambulatory vehicle great but a wheelchair vehicle amazing [VGWUx-p8MbM @ 00:02:02]. RouteGenie backs the wheelchair side on volume. It warns that limiting yourself to ambulatory passengers will probably mean fewer available contracts, and cites Indiana figures of 63.5% ambulatory and 30.3% wheelchair requests to argue that a minivan can complete up to 90% of contracts [Lh999r_-mi0 @ 00:04:07]. At the premium end of the market, RouteGenie's 2026 buyer guide lists access to higher-paying contracts for full-size stretcher vans. The same guide notes that stretcher transport represents only about 10% of orders, against higher purchase price, fuel consumption, and maintenance costs [uJV2f3MOJbI @ 00:06:25]. The playbook that reconciles these positions is Nemt University's own six-month plan: start on a personal vehicle, then step up to a wheelchair van if business goes well, with market research deciding the timing.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is underestimating what a van costs to keep on the road. NEMT Growth Machine bought a Ford Transit 350 XL with a rear wheelchair lift for $87,900 after taxes and put $6,000 down. The van payment now runs about $1,600 a month. The owners call commercial insurance the killer: about $17,315 a year, or roughly $1,440 a month. Together those push fixed costs right above $3,000 a month before oil changes, tire rotations, or gas [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:00:20]. Their all-in estimate lands around $43,000 a year, rounded to $45,000 once unexpected maintenance enters. They offset fuel by charging for mileage on longer runs to Matthews and Concord [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:06:40]. Nemt University warns financed buyers to confirm during market research that revenue can cover both the note and the insurance, because those can get quite expensive [VGWUx-p8MbM @ 00:05:43]. RouteGenie flags a used-market trap that bites budget buyers. The Dodge Grand Caravan was sold exclusively as a fleet vehicle in its final years, so extremely low prices might signal poor condition; used 2019 units normally run $13,000 to $16,000 [uJV2f3MOJbI @ 00:03:21]. Run the payment, insurance, and mileage math before signing, not after the first slow month.

The second trap is the dead mile. LearnCargo says the cancellation call almost never comes. Nine times out of 10, the driver finds out at the last minute on their own, sometimes because the broker never passed the cancellation along. The fix is calling the broker to get a note placed on that client's account after driving 30 miles for nothing [MOdO2Zzw1wI @ 00:01:02]. RouteGenie frames the cost as scheduling gaps and lost revenue. It estimates that an operator facing more than one no-show a month could be losing upwards of a thousand dollars monthly, and cites research tying up to 31.5% of no-shows to poor provider communication [R4q_XZ1pARQ @ 00:01:59]. Its cancellation playbook asks passengers to cancel at least 24 hours before pickup, and gives the example of a $25 fee on a $100 trip canceled within 24 hours. It warns that disputes over no-show charges are common unless the policy is written, published, and enforced consistently, with fee waivers spelled out in advance [d8ocN3ERJag @ 00:04:22]. MJ Business Academy shows the field version. Their client agreed to pay wait time if not outside at the 10:30 pickup, so the clock starts the moment the van arrives and the client is not ready [ohTDpW0zUS8 @ 00:05:37].

The third trap is buying a van that turns trips away or fails mid-run. MJ Business Academy, five years into operating, says rehabilitation center patients often ride with leg extenders that a smaller wheelchair van cannot fit, so that is one trip you will have to turn away. The same tight cabin blocks multi-loading and husband-and-wife wheelchair pairs. It also leaves the wheelchair parked where it takes the brunt of a rear impact [P_pN6quM3G4 @ 00:03:02]. Jasmine and Monica also show how thin punctuality margins are. They rolled up to St. JW Medical Plaza one minute late for a 10:30 pickup with a client who likes them on time, blaming a business call that ran long [ohTDpW0zUS8 @ 00:02:34]. Cleanup is another hidden failure point. Their full cut Caravan has no carpet because clients have accidents and leak bodily fluids, so the floor wipes clean [rIDRpTROLM8 @ 00:01:32]. NEMT Growth Machine stocks a duffel with gloves, N95 masks, a first aid kit, and a bloodborne pathogen spill kit. The van also carries a jack, a spare tire, and three reflective triangles set roughly 10, 100, and 200 feet behind a disabled van. They do this even on 2025 Transits they say should not have issues [nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:04:26].

callout.title: Four Checks Before the Van Rolls
callout.body: Clear these four practitioner-tested checks before committing capital to a vehicle or dispatching the first trip of the day.
items: Price the full monthly burn, a payment near $1,600 plus insurance near $1,440, before signing the note [NEMT Growth Machine — nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:00:20].
Confirm your state accepts the entry style, since California denied a rear entry van without an emergency exit for Medicaid wheelchair work [MJ Business Academy — P_pN6quM3G4 @ 00:11:02].
Measure the van against your actual client base, including leg extenders, reclining wheelchairs, and couples who both ride in wheelchairs [MJ Business Academy — ohTDpW0zUS8 @ 00:06:54].
Publish a written no-show and cancellation policy built on a 24-hour notice window, and turn on automated trip reminders [RouteGenie — d8ocN3ERJag @ 00:02:26].

chapters.pull_quote: “Please stop buying rear entry wheelchair vans. Like if you're going to take the non-emergency medical transportation industry serious, you need to have a serious vehicle.” — Wheelchair & Stretcher Transportation Services (svdIU5f-6tA @ 00:00:03)
action_checklist: Set a hard vehicle budget of $7,500, $10,000, or $20,000, and decide between cash, financing, or a lease before shopping [Nemt University — VGWUx-p8MbM @ 00:04:37].
Walk the van at a mobility dealership with a rep who lays out the advantages and disadvantages of extended versus smaller cuts [MJ Business Academy — P_pN6quM3G4 @ 00:10:25].
Benchmark used pricing before buying, such as $25,000 to $30,000 for a 2019 Ford Transit against new pricing from $50,500 [RouteGenie — uJV2f3MOJbI @ 00:08:49].

Stock the van with a phone mount, dash and interior cameras, Clorox wipes, an umbrella, a fire extinguisher, a spill kit, reflective triangles, and business cards [NEMT Growth Machine — nSB43YYfRs0 @ 00:02:25].
Run a pre-trip inspection of fluids, tire pressure, brakes, lights, wheelchair lifts, and securement straps before the 4 or 5 a.m. first pickup [RouteGenie — qiZqLls0G-E @ 00:03:23].
Tell every rider to call the broker when they will not travel, and log broker notification failures on the client's account [LearnCargo — MOdO2Zzw1wI @ 00:00:32].

chapters.question_prompt: How do Medicaid NEMT brokers work, how do I get in network, and how do I protect myself from broker tactics?
chapters.title: Working With (and Around) Medicaid Brokers
chapters.subtitle: Finding and inquiring with brokers, the four broker payment models (fee-for-service, capitation, MCO, hybrid), broker lists, Modivcare's NC takeover, Georgia's 2.1M-ride award, the $200K loss and $75K MTM fines case, contract and service agreement terms, renewal retaliation, VA third-party contract traps, and operating out of network
chapters.executive_summary: Medicaid brokers sit between state Medicaid money and the van owner. They collect the full reimbursement and subpay providers a lower number. Nemiton puts that spread at 15-35%, and WholeRoute says 60-80% gets taken out. MJ Business Academy, WholeRoute, Nemiton and Joel Davis of UMTPG agree that broker trips are easy to get, cheap, and dangerous to depend on. The street mechanics include inquiry forms resubmitted weekly, calls to the broker before applying, credentialing windows of 21-45 days, and mileage-bucket rates from a $7.23 base up to a $55-70 wheelchair base. Davis negotiates hard, in writing only, and pushes email-only correspondence, cherry-picked trips and out-of-network leverage. Christopher Buell and Six Figure Transportation's Eric skip brokers almost entirely. Nemiton models a 70/30 broker/private hybrid that adds about $6,000 a month.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus: Brokers Are Volume at a Discount, Never the Foundation
paragraphs: A Medicaid broker is the middleman between the state's Medicaid money and the provider who actually runs the van, and every practitioner here describes the same economics [0nJ9GYcr744 @ 00:01:21]. Nemiton lays it out plainly: the broker receives the state's full Medicaid reimbursement rate and subpays the provider at a lower number. That spread runs 15-35%, which works out to $15,000-18,750 a year on a 3-vehicle fleet [LjAb-IUYxbM @ 00:01:11]. Jay at WholeRoute puts the cut even higher. Statistically, he says, 60 to 80% gets taken out before the provider sees a dollar [rLXiXIWHxIA @ 00:03:12]. Joel Davis of UMTPG adds the piece most newcomers miss: the broker still gets paid for trips that are not performed, and the provider does not. Cancellations and no-shows therefore become free money on the broker's side of the ledger [Bvcsc1hEgT0 @ 00:12:00]. In the same breakdown Davis describes the payment chain. The true guaranteed payer is the government, and the government guarantees it will pay the broker. The broker never guarantees it will pay you. He tells providers to negotiate no-show pay whenever they have the leverage. The shared conclusion is that broker work is real, steady volume, but it is priced at a structural discount. A broker is a pipe for trips, not a partner, and operators who treat it as anything more get squeezed.

The second point of agreement is that brokers should be a slice of the business, never the foundation. Jasmine and Monica of MJ Business Academy tell new owners to keep brokers to a small share of revenue, because brokers themselves can lose their health-plan contracts and take your volume with them [KSSO5Igfn2Y @ 00:09:55]. Jay at WholeRoute sizes the broker at "maybe 15 maybe 20%" of potential revenue and uses website and community-rider math to fill the rest [rLXiXIWHxIA @ 00:20:22]. Nemiton calls broker concentration the number one hidden risk in NEMT [LjAb-IUYxbM @ 00:13:47]. Joel Davis supplies the casualties. One client lost about $185K after buying the wrong vehicles on bad advice and is still waiting on about $45K from ModivCare. A second client faces an MTM audit claiming $75K on disputed trips worth roughly $20K, plus a demand for flat rates. Both were 100% broker-dependent [A2vs7pLblSk @ 00:12:13]. Davis calls these agreements "sharecropping" and says Medicaid-heavy companies carry the lowest resale value in NEMT. His fix is to keep using the existing Medicaid cash flow while signing direct-pay contracts with hospitals, SNFs and schools. Everyone who addresses the question lands in the same place: take the broker money, but plan your exit away from it from day one.

The baseline prerequisites are the same on every channel. Nemt University lists an NPI from cms.gov, an EIN, and an LLC or corporation as the entry ticket before any broker conversation [0nJ9GYcr744 @ 00:04:31]. Nemt University also splits the landscape into four models [iihLkCuH8NY @ 00:01:12]:
- In-house state management on fee-for-service, which the speaker calls "the best one." Examples: Michigan, Pennsylvania and Minnesota.
- MCO managed care, where trips need prior approval that owners dislike.
- Statewide or regional brokers that centralize call centers, eligibility and authorization. Examples: Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina, Louisiana and Texas.
- Mixed county-by-county models such as Philadelphia County.
Nemiton opens its own breakdown with a warning: if you signed a broker contract without knowing which of the four models you operate under, you do not know your business [LjAb-IUYxbM @ 00:00:00]. Georgia's transition to Verida shows what full broker requirements look like in practice. They include GAMMIS enrollment, a Type 2 NPI, and $1M auto plus $1M general liability per occurrence with Verida and DCH named as additional insureds. Vehicles must be 2016 or newer, lift-equipped and GPS-tracked. Drivers must clear a 3-year MVR, FBI fingerprints, and HIPAA, ADA, CPR and first aid training [zXw7440bths @ 00:07:31]. Nemt University also sees consolidation coming, with brokers shrinking toward 3 national players.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: Getting In, Pricing, and Operating on Your Terms
paragraphs:
Getting onto a broker panel is a paperwork grind with a sales layer on top. MJ Business Academy's workflow is simple. Go to each broker's website, click the inquiry tab, and fill out the questionnaire. Pre-launch owners can describe themselves as a current provider ("you have two vehicles") [KSSO5Igfn2Y @ 00:01:33]. Expect a reply in 5-7 business days listing the required documents. If nothing comes back, resubmit every week, because inquiries get lost [KSSO5Igfn2Y @ 00:03:35]. Jay at WholeRoute insists you call the broker before you apply and ask three questions [rLXiXIWHxIA @ 00:12:49]:
1. Are you accepting providers, and what is the trip volume?
2. What vehicle types do you need?
3. What are the insurance requirements?
On the application, list a routing or dispatch software and present your driving experience competitively, though Jay says not to lie. Have a website ready, because half of brokers require one. Plan for a long timeline. Jay budgets about 3 months to get in. In one Florida case, a provider with 2 ambulatory vehicles was asked for 4 wheelchair vehicles after waiting 4 months. Only half of applicants get a contract at all [rLXiXIWHxIA @ 00:11:48]. Brokers mostly add providers when enrollment rises. A provider exit creating a vacuum is a "1%" case, and 80-85% of applicants are first-time owners competing against established taxi fleets.

Rates are where, in MJ Business Academy's words, "the battle starts." Never accept the first offer, and keep pushing until the broker says "final final offer" [KSSO5Igfn2Y @ 00:05:52]. Broker pay comes in mileage buckets. Trips of 0-3 miles start around $12, rates climb to $26-27 on longer buckets, and an ambulatory 5-mile round trip lands around "30 something 40." Wheelchair pays more than ambulatory. The low end is brutal. The Southeast Trans sheet Joel Davis reviewed set ambulatory at a $7.23 base with 6 miles included and $1.32 a mile after, and wheelchair at a $17 base with 6 miles included and $1.48 a mile after [v-IpSBjauKY @ 00:03:12]. A ModivCare holdout in the same video was paid a 14 base and $1.65 a mile ambulatory, and an 18 base and $1.85 a mile wheelchair, with no increase since 2019. Georgia under Verida pays more. Ambulatory runs $28-35 base plus $1.35-1.85 a mile, and wheelchair $55-70 base plus $2.75 a mile. Private facility rates there are $65 ambulatory and $95 wheelchair. Verida pays net 21 to net 30 and audits heavily in the first 90 days [zXw7440bths @ 00:11:35]. For rate reviews, Nemiton's leverage list is an on-time rate above 95%, a low no-show rate, a review request at 6 months, and a push for multi-year terms [LjAb-IUYxbM @ 00:14:39].

How you behave inside a broker relationship matters as much as the rate. Davis and his UMTPG team insist that all correspondence with ModivCare go by email. Brokers push for phone calls because it is part of their training, and calls leave no paper trail [0Z6CsGngipI @ 00:02:44]. Davis plays deliberately hard to get over email. He calls the broker a "pet alligator": you can be friendly with it, but it is not your friend. He advises staying out of network unless the margin is good. One out-of-network operator shows the payoff. Brokers offered to raise that operator's rates, Access2Care offered to remove the mileage cap on stretcher rates, and MTM put a credit card on file for a dialysis client [xx3dHh731rY @ 00:05:46]. That operator runs about 10 vehicles at seven-figure revenue and roughly 50% margin, against Davis's target of about 25%. Inside the network, Davis says to cherry-pick and skip the losing trips [Bvcsc1hEgT0 @ 00:14:51]. Brokers police providers in return. MTM Michigan's rules [Bvcsc1hEgT0 @ 00:04:14]:
- No quoting on trips; only Schedule A rates apply.
- Every vendor no-show gets a follow-up call.
- More than 5 complaints a month triggers a call.
- Turn-backs are reviewed daily, and capacity is cut.
- High numbers for over 2 months lead to a corrective action plan, then termination.
Davis also warns never to depend on broker software, because brokers eventually lose their contracts.

callout.title: How the Veterans Work the Broker Without Getting Eaten
callout.body: These moves come straight from operators who have negotiated, declined, or worked outside broker contracts. Each one protects margin, leverage, or the paper trail.
items: Keep every broker exchange in writing. Brokers push for phone calls because it is part of their training, so stay off the phones and correspond by email [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — 0Z6CsGngipI @ 00:04:36].

If the broker reaches out first, you are "in the driver's seat." Play hard to get over email and work out of network unless the margin is good [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — 0Z6CsGngipI @ 00:06:21].
Pick software that integrates with brokers instead of running on theirs. RouteGenie integrates with MTM, ModivCare and Access2Care [Nemiton — LjAb-IUYxbM @ 00:16:01].

Use social services as a side door. Vance County Social Services needs providers and pays more than ModivCare, and working directly with social services usually means better rates [Motivational Charles — BCwbkTt30cY @ 00:03:57].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether a broker belongs in the business at all. Christopher Buell grew one company to about 10 vans in roughly four years and a second to about 8 vans in roughly two and a half years, predominantly without brokers, and calls the DHS-to-broker bidding setup in that state totally not worth it; the preferred move is collecting payment on the spot and handing the client a receipt to submit to their insurance [HxtN-7tsjNA @ 00:05:27]. Eric at Six Figure Transportation does not work with brokers at all, steering into skilled nursing facilities where 5 to 10 percent of residents are temporary rehab patients who become private-pay riders on automatic after discharge [zyo_6OZNupU @ 00:02:15]. The middle camp keeps the broker but shrinks it. Jasmine and Monica tell owners to keep brokers a small share of revenue because brokers can lose their health-plan contracts [KSSO5Igfn2Y @ 00:09:55], while Joel Davis tells fully broker-dependent clients to leverage existing Medicaid cash flow as the bankroll for direct-pay hospital, SNF, and school contracts instead of walking away cold [A2vs7pLblSk @ 00:33:56]. The real choice is how much runway the private book has before broker money dries up, not which camp sounds tougher.

Practitioners also split on how loud to negotiate. Jasmine and Monica treat rate talks as the moment when the battle starts: never accept the first offer, keep pushing until the broker says final final offer, and expect mileage buckets that open near $12 for 0 to 3 miles and climb to $26 or $27 [KSSO5Igfn2Y @ 00:05:52]. Joel Davis plays it colder. The Davis rule is he who speaks first loses, and when a welcome packet forces you to show retail prices first, you come in strong [gJ4V8yGqCFY @ 00:00:43]. With brokers specifically, Davis runs a deliberate hard-to-get email strategy and keeps every exchange in writing, because brokers are trained to pull providers onto the phone where no paper trail exists [0Z6CsGngipI @ 00:04:36]. Nemiton offers a data-driven third path: walk in with an on-time rate above 95 percent and a low no-show rate, request a rate review after six months, push for multi-year terms, and expect some brokers to counter with volume guarantees instead of higher per-trip pay [LjAb-IUYxbM @ 00:14:39]. The tradeoff is visible: the push-hard camp chases rate bumps on the call, while the paper-trail camp protects the provider when a later audit or penalty dispute lands.

Where to plug in is the third fault line. Nemt University ranks the in-house model, where the State Medicaid agency administers NEMT fee-for-service, as the best one, naming Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Minnesota, and notes owners do not like the prior approvals that come with MCO work [iihLkCuH8NY @ 00:01:12]. Nemiton instead maps payers to fleet size: one to three vehicles run FFS in tier-1 states or MCO in tier-3 states, four to ten vehicles stack MCO with private pay, and eleven-plus go full hybrid with no single payer above 60 percent [LjAb-IUYxbM @ 00:12:41]. Joel Davis pushes the out-of-network route unless broker margin is good, pointing to clients who operate out of network yet still hold a broker credit card on file, while conceding the play fails in markets saturated with independents [0Z6CsGngipI @ 00:06:21]. Motivational Charles, boxed out because North Carolina Social Services enrollment is closed and ModivCare holds all the PHP plans, is emailing Vance County Social Services because it needs providers and pays more than ModivCare [BCwbkTt30cY @ 00:03:57]. Same goal, four different doors: state FFS, model-matched contracts, out-of-network leverage, or county-direct billing, and each depends on what the local market actually allows.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure is total broker dependence. Joel Davis walked through a client who lost about $185K after buying the wrong vehicles on bad advice and is still waiting on roughly $45K from ModivCare, alongside a second client whose MTM audit claims $75K owed on disputed trips worth about $20K while demanding flat rates; Davis calls broker agreements sharecropping and notes both clients were 100 percent broker-dependent [A2vs7pLblSk @ 00:09:40]. A taxi company turned NEMT provider running 25 to 40 legs a day across 50 counties with LogistiCare got the same verdict: the house is completely built on sand [xx3dHh731rY @ 00:20:18]. Davis also warns against leaning on broker software, because brokers eventually lose their contracts and a provider wired into their systems collapses with them [Bvcsc1hEgT0 @ 00:06:22]. Nemt University puts a number on that churn: Verida takes all five Georgia regions on April 1, 2026 as ModivCare exits, and about 30 percent of providers fail to re-credential in time after a broker switch, with credentialing alone taking 21 to 45 days [zXw7440bths @ 00:06:26]. The check is blunt: if one broker transition or one audit letter can choke cash flow, broker share is too high.

The second trap is signing or renewing at rates that cannot carry the truck. Davis showed a Southeast Trans offer a provider was pushed to sign on January 12: ambulatory at a $7.23 base with six miles included and $1.32 per mile after, wheelchair at $17 base with the same six miles and $1.48 per mile [v-IpSBjauKY @ 00:03:12]. A ModivCare holdout on 14 base at $1.65 per mile had seen no increase since 2019 despite gas and labor costs, had done no hospital or nursing-home outreach in that stretch, and now faced a late-renewal penalty of up to $2,500 a month [v-IpSBjauKY @ 00:20:18]. Travae Willis reports North Carolina insurance rising about 40 percent and companies going out of business because of it, so the advice is stay small and price trips to cover insurance [YFWOnVDBziM @ 00:08:10]. Under all of it sits the leakage brokers keep: they get paid for trips that are not performed while the provider does not, which is why Davis says to negotiate no-show pay whenever you hold leverage [Bvcsc1hEgT0 @ 00:12:00]. Run the per-trip math against insurance, fuel, and driver cost before the signature, not after the first quarter.

The third cluster is launch and operating mistakes that kill new entrants. WholeRoute's Jay says only half of applicants land a broker contract and 70 percent of those are out of business within the first year, with 80 to 85 percent of new applicants being first-time business owners competing against established taxi fleets [rLXiXIWHxIA @ 00:02:01]. Davis warns off both ends of the vehicle market, new vans at $80K to $100K-plus and $5K clunkers, after a client's $185K loss tied to the wrong vehicles [A2vs7pLblSk @ 00:13:31]. On the VA side, Travae Willis says the callers asking about your van count and rates are usually management firms with no vans that win the SAM.gov bid and pay pennies on the dollar, and that even a seasoned operator with about 18 vans could not handle a roughly 20,000-trip-a-year contract [YFWOnVDBziM @ 00:06:44]. Once inside a broker network, enforcement bites: the MTM Michigan letter bans trip quoting, triggers calls at more than five complaints a month, reviews turn-backs daily, and moves high numbers lasting over two months to a corrective action plan and then termination [Bvcsc1hEgT0 @ 00:12:50]. Capacity, vehicles, and metrics have to be squared before chasing volume.

callout.title: Before You Sign or Renew With a Broker
callout.body: Every item below comes from a provider who already paid for skipping it. Clear all four before the signature goes on a broker agreement or renewal.
items: Broker share check: if one broker is 100 percent of revenue, you are in the same seat as the clients who lost about $185K and faced a $75K MTM audit claim [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — A2vs7pLblSk @ 00:12:13].

Paper trail check: every broker exchange on rates, renewals, and disputes goes by email, never phone, so you have a paper trail [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — 0Z6CsGngipI @ 00:22:59].
Re-credential check: the moment a broker switch is announced, start credentialing, because about 30 percent of providers miss the window [Nemt University — zXw7440bths @ 00:06:26].

Vehicle cash check: put vehicles and capital equipment in a separate entity that leases them to the NEMT business, and buy future vehicles in cash after P&L and cash-flow review [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — v-IpSBjauKY @ 00:34:28].

action_checklist: Call the broker before applying and ask whether they are accepting providers, the trip volume, the vehicle types needed, and the insurance requirements [WholeRoute — rLXiXIWHxIA @ 00:12:49].
Fill out the broker inquiry questionnaire, expect a document list in 5 to 7 business days, and resubmit every week if no reply arrives [MJ Business Academy — KSSO5Igfn2Y @ 00:03:35].
Move all broker correspondence to email and refuse phone-based negotiation so every rate and dispute has a paper trail [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — 0Z6CsGngipI @ 00:04:36].
Back every rate request with an on-time rate above 95 percent and a low no-show rate, and request a rate review after six months [Nemiton — LjAb-IUYxbM @ 00:14:39].
Cherry-pick trips, refuse loser trips, and negotiate paid no-shows whenever you hold leverage [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — Bvcsc1hEgT0 @ 00:14:51].
Get out from behind the desk and visit facilities in person to land direct service agreements outside the broker [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — 0Z6CsGngipI @ 00:20:37].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I win private pay clients, facility contracts, and direct referrals without relying on brokers?
chapters.title: Private Pay, Facility Contracts, and Direct Referral Pipelines
chapters.subtitle: Brokers vs. private pay, 30+ private pay revenue streams, landing nursing home and rehab contracts, first 10 clients without a broker, direct referral systems, winning dialysis rides from the broker, facilities paying directly despite Medicaid/Medicare residents, negotiation leverage, hospitals paying $6K/day for discharges, and a $2M/year stretcher discharge operation
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners running broker-light NEMT shops converge on one thesis: direct facility contracts and private-pay riders carry the margin, while brokers act as toll booths. Nemiton pegs broker-only margins at 5-15% versus 25-40% for diversified operators, with in-person facility visits closing 30-50% of the time. United Medical Transportation Providers Group reports an East Coast hospital system spending $6,000 per weekday on discharge transport and wanting one provider to capture it all, while Bambi guest Mike Boron runs stretcher-focused discharges at an average $230 per 7-mile trip. The street playbook is presence: morning visits, snacks, honest pickup windows, after-hours coverage, and prepayment. Disagreement centers on brokers, which MJ Business Academy and Nemiton still treat as a scaling or negotiating slice, and on facility payment risk, from net-30 delays to chargebacks and pulled contracts.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Operators who have pulled volume away from brokers agree on one blunt thesis: direct facility and private-pay work is where NEMT margin lives. Nemiton says broker-only businesses live on 5-15% margins, while owners diversified into direct facility and private pay run 25-40%, which it calls triple the margin [6nWzJ25nMDg @ 00:00:36]. Stephanie on Zenpath Radio puts it in dollars: a broker may pay $25, and a $10 difference is a huge gap when you think about profit, so the plan was to wean brokers out of the revenue pie and take broker trips only when a van is already nearby [VOkoxr2bB2Q @ 00:23:05]. Tony Jackson, operations manager at Top Choice Medical Transport in Orlando with 25 years in NEMT, runs almost entirely private pay with 0% broker work because brokers keep all the money [ICI0C5f_vjE @ 00:21:01]. Mike Boron of Ambiance Medical Transportation bought a company that was about 90% broker, exited broker wheelchair rides paying $27, absorbed the hit when brokers stopped handing out the gurney trips they used as a reward for taking wheelchairs, and now runs at a 4-5% broker share [bGYVSmlvo90 @ 00:01:47]. The shared lesson across all four shops is that rate control, not raw trip count, decides whether a van actually earns money.

The second point of agreement is that contracts are won by physical presence and relationship equity, not ads or scripts. Jasmine and Monica of MJ Business Academy, who run MJ Reliable Transportation in California, say they win contracts by being present, showing up, being reliable and following up; when a resident gets picked up weekly from a non-contracted facility, they introduce themselves every morning, engage the staff until the staff likes them, and only then ask whether an agreement can be put in place [LCV7CgKI3PQ @ 00:00:22]. Nemiton's six-step system, drawn from owners who scaled past 15 vehicles, starts with in-person visits and cites one owner who built a half-million-dollar operation in 24 months on take snacks, introduce yourself, follow up [6nWzJ25nMDg @ 00:01:31]. Nemt Business Life, which grew from 100% self-pay to 20 facility contracts, argues that the patient's opinion is the most powerful part of getting that new contract, which turns rider experience into the deciding factor [UtiLgcZo4dU @ 00:18:10]. Even the PractiScale vendor pitch for outsourced outreach concedes the provider still has to build the relationship after the call is booked, calling referral partners the most stable way to grow [R0U1p8_k4J0 @ 00:04:18]. The common thread is repetition: the same faces, the same staff, every week.

The baseline prerequisites are just as consistent. First, match the fleet to the target: MJ Business Academy warns ambulatory-only providers to skip hospice, which needs a gurney, and hospitals, whose discharges need a wheelchair or gurney, or those callers are eventually going to stop calling; they steer ambulatory vans toward same-day routine-surgery clinics instead [bX8mww6N5BM @ 00:07:33]. Second, rank targets by recurrence rather than prestige. Nemiton puts dialysis first because it generates multiple trips per week indefinitely, followed by rehab, hospitals through discharge planners, senior living and specialty clinics such as oncology [6nWzJ25nMDg @ 00:00:57]. Nemt Business Life backs the ranking from the churn side: only dialysis and cancer patients stay long-term on private pay, while others recover or shift to Medi-Cal [UtiLgcZo4dU @ 00:04:21]. Third, find the gap the incumbent leaves open instead of fighting for the slot it already holds. Marcus of All American Health, on the Wheelchair & Stretcher Transportation Services channel, notes that facilities with in-house vans staff them with an 8-to-5 employee, so nobody covers after 5 PM, and that gap is the follow-up when a facility says it already has a transportation provider [zn8XUaFzOCk @ 00:00:39]. Marcus frames the whole job bluntly: you are a solutions business, not a transportation company.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The pipeline mechanics are specific. Nemt University tells operators to open Google Maps and physically visit everything within a 10-mile radius, asking for the social worker or transportation director [yrd3dFXxLmw @ 00:02:27]. Nemiton's numbers justify the legwork: in-person facility visits close 30-50% of the time, referrals close 40-60%, and waiting on brokers closes nothing, while most new owners burn their first six months waiting [6nWzJ25nMDg @ 00:00:00]. Its sequence runs identify facilities in your radius, visit in person, hold a discovery call that listens first and asks what breaks, such as late pickups, no-shows and wheelchair gaps, do a site visit, send a custom proposal instead of a rate sheet, and close with a 30-60 day pilot; no step requires money, and ten clients take roughly 20-30 conversations, doable in three weeks. MJ Business Academy adds canvassing nursing homes, hospitals, dialysis clinics and skilled nursing facilities with brochures and business cards, plus cold calling facilities, the same technique a real-estate follower of theirs had not realized carries over to NEMT [bX8mww6N5BM @ 00:04:05]. Duet NEMT goes after dialysis riders the broker strands for 2-3 hours, asking clinics to let flyers sit out so those patients can call and pay out of pocket [caWAkt063_Q @ 00:00:31].

Pricing and payment terms are where the money gets protected. MJ Business Academy's rule is that you should not be doing a trip if you did not receive payment before that trip when no contract exists; cancellations within 24 hours get a full refund minus a processing fee of a couple of dollars, and any facility 45 days past due goes to upfront payment on new trips [LCV7CgKI3PQ @ 00:04:38]. They also offer a 15% discount in exchange for exclusivity, with the warning that you better be ready to cover every trip. Mike Boron prices stretcher discharges from a floor of about $180 for 3 miles to an average of $230 for 7 miles including wait, undercutting ambulance bills that run up to $1,600 on weekends by charging $250-300, and refuses health-plan offers of $110 per discharge because you cannot make money at 100 [bGYVSmlvo90 @ 00:10:53]. Joel Davis of United Medical Transportation Providers Group walked a one-vehicle client through a nursing facility agreement where corporate legal tried net-60; the client pushed back across several rounds, and the agreement reads invoices due by the third business day with net-30 payment [FKvCovIVs3Q @ 00:09:26]. Joel's rule: negotiations are 10 to 20% tops, terms are 80% of how you play the game.

The tooling is lean and service-driven. Tony Jackson says Bambi cut trip entry from about 5 minutes to 2-3, and the Run Bambi Run auto-scheduler cut a one-hour scheduling job to 5 minutes with minimal manual edits; drivers run tablets instead of phones, and daily trips at the 14-vehicle shop went from about 20 to 75 within a month [ICI0C5f_vjE @ 00:22:23]. Mike Boron sells reliability as product: 2-hour guaranteed windows, a never-leave-a-patient rule, EMT attendants even though they are not required, and a facility portal that gives hospitals live vehicle tracking [bGYVSmlvo90 @ 00:19:32]. MJ Business Academy keeps software to scheduling only, MediRoutes and Route Genie, and tells operators to stay away from the mobile apps that push trips, because taking app trips turns you into a contracted driver instead of your own boss [bX8mww6N5BM @ 00:11:31]. Sherry C. Wright of Campton Transport in Birmingham, on Zenpath Radio, applies a hard dispatch filter: only take a trip if a van can reach the client within 20 minutes of the call, and on dialysis days the first pickup is 4:40 because the center opens at 5 [_BmJ_SxXCUY @ 00:04:25]. Each standard doubles as proof to a facility that the operator will actually show up.

callout.title: Street Tactics That Open Facility Doors
callout.body: The operators pulling direct volume use objections, honesty and audit fear as entry points rather than discounting their way in.
items: When a facility says 'we already have a transportation provider,' answer 'perfect, who does your after-hours work?' and make that your follow-up [Wheelchair & Stretcher Transportation Services — zn8XUaFzOCk @ 00:02:08]

Quote honest pickup windows such as '3 to 3:30' instead of a false '2:00'; Tony Jackson says honesty goes a long way and facilities follow the provider giving great customer service [Bambi — ICI0C5f_vjE @ 00:10:43]

Even when a dialysis clinic routes rides through the broker, seed the idea that riders request your service by name, and post hours that cover the 5:00 a.m. dialysis runs [Duet NEMT — caWAkt063_Q @ 00:00:46]

Use ER audit exposure as leverage in hospital talks: bill Medicaid when the patient is fully covered, otherwise the hospital pays you directly and avoids fines [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — HvP2_Kts7vA @ 00:11:30]

sop_steps.title: Map and walk the radius
sop_steps.action: Pull every facility within 10 miles on Google Maps and visit each one in person.
sop_steps.detail: Ask for the social worker or transportation director, and work dialysis, rehab, discharge planners and senior living first because they recur [Nemt University — yrd3dFXxLmw @ 00:02:27]

sop_steps.title: Run the discovery call
sop_steps.action: Listen first and ask what breaks before pitching anything.
sop_steps.detail: Probe late pickups, no-shows and wheelchair gaps, then do a site visit and send a custom proposal instead of a rate sheet [Nemiton — 6nWzJ25nMDg @ 00:01:31]

sop_steps.title: Pilot, then paper the deal
sop_steps.action: Run a 30-60 day pilot and convert it into a written agreement with tight terms.
sop_steps.detail: Push for invoices due by the third business day with net-30 payment and refuse net-60, since terms are 80% of how you play the game [United Medical Transportation Providers Group — FKvCovIVs3Q @ 00:09:26]

sop_steps.title: Lock in cash collection
sop_steps.action: Collect prepayment on every non-contract trip and enforce a past-due trigger on facilities.
sop_steps.detail: No payment before the trip means no trip, and any invoice 45 days past due moves that facility to upfront payment on new trips [MJ Business Academy — LCV7CgKI3PQ @ 00:04:38]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
sections.title: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is how much broker volume an operator should keep. Jasmine and Monica of MJ Business Academy treat brokers as a scaling engine, reporting operators who went from one vehicle to four or five in three months, while still telling owners to stack private pay and multiple income streams on top [bX8mww6N5BM @ 00:10:34]. Nemiton formalizes that hedge as the 33/33/33 model: one-third broker, one-third direct facility, one-third private pay, with the balance itself creating negotiating power and private pay delivering the fastest, highest-margin dollars [6nWzJ25nMDg @ 00:04:48]. Tony Jackson of Top Choice Medical Transport sits at the opposite pole, running the Orlando operation almost entirely on private pay with 0% broker work because 'Brokers keep all the money' [ICI0C5f_vjE @ 00:21:01]. Joel Davis of United Medical Transportation Providers Group goes furthest, telling operators to stop asking for help landing Modivcare or MTM contracts and branding brokers 'toll booth operators' standing between the provider and the money [HvP2_Kts7vA @ 00:09:07]. The scaling camp prizes immediate trip flow while the direct-only camp prizes rate control and margin, yet nobody on either side recommends living on broker dispatch alone; every speaker builds a private-pay lane alongside whatever broker volume they tolerate.

Pricing philosophy splits three ways. Nemt University pitches private pay as the route to higher rates, stressing that rates are negotiable directly between the provider and the particular medical facility, with no broker schedule capping the number [yrd3dFXxLmw @ 00:02:11]. Nemt Business Life pushes back from the experience of running 20 facility contracts: facilities work off budgets and an operator will get outbid, so the play is pricing in the middle, high enough to still cover repairs, permits, and gas while staying in contention [UtiLgcZo4dU @ 00:06:06]. MJ Business Academy goes the other direction for one specific structure, offering a 15% discount in exchange for an exclusive contract, with the blunt condition that 'you better be ready' to cover every trip the facility sends [LCV7CgKI3PQ @ 00:10:17]. Joel Davis frames the rate as the minor lever entirely: negotiations are 10 to 20% of the outcome 'tops,' and terms are 80% of how you play the game, which is why the client fought corporate legal over payment terms across several rounds [FKvCovIVs3Q @ 00:05:13]. Read together, discounting belongs only where fleet capacity can absorb exclusivity, premium pricing belongs where the facility has no reliable alternative, and middle pricing is the default when a budgeted buyer is shopping several providers.

Outreach method is the third fault line. MJ Business Academy tells operators to cold call facilities the same way real-estate agents work leads, alongside canvassing nursing homes, hospitals, dialysis clinics, and skilled nursing facilities with brochures and business cards [bX8mww6N5BM @ 00:05:02]. Joel Davis rejects the scripted version outright: buying call scripts is not a strategy for building, scaling, and selling at a future multiple, a script will not motivate a case manager or unit secretary, and faxing business cards is 'nonsense' [PVivs9VOAyw @ 00:01:49]. Nemiton puts numbers on the face-to-face route: in-person facility visits close 30 to 50% of the time, referrals close 40 to 60%, and waiting on brokers closes nothing, yet most new owners burn their first six months waiting anyway [6nWzJ25nMDg @ 00:00:00]. PractiScale sells the opposite of doing it yourself, a done-for-you service that identifies hospitals, dialysis centers, nursing homes, and discharge planners, reaches out on the provider's behalf, and books calls so the owner only has to build the relationship [R0U1p8_k4J0 @ 00:03:27]. The common thread is that a human referral source controls the trips; the dispute is whether the owner earns that seat in person, dials for it, or pays a third party to open the door.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
sections.title: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Getting paid is where facility contracts break first. MJ Business Academy warns that facilities take 30 days to pay and sometimes miss even that, and Jasmine and Monica are carrying a non-paying facility they have called repeatedly over a couple of weeks, knowing that cutting off a non-payer can mean never recouping the money [LCV7CgKI3PQ @ 00:02:44]. Their in-house fix splits: Monica refuses to run more trips, while Jasmine's counter is to quote $625 for three clients, stack the $3,000 past-due balance on top, and run 'three thousand six' on the card in one charge [LCV7CgKI3PQ @ 00:07:42]. Private pay carries its own reversal risk. Nemt Business Life lost money when a discharged patient told the bank the charges were unknown and the bank refunded them, which is exactly the dispute MJ's collect-before-the-trip rule is built to block [UtiLgcZo4dU @ 00:09:35]. Even signed paper is a fight: Joel Davis watched a large nursing facility's corporate legal team rewrite a one-vehicle client's agreement and try to slip in net-60 terms, forcing the client to push back across several rounds [FKvCovIVs3Q @ 00:04:14]. The economics check from the MJ camp is blunt: keep other income streams running so one slow-paying facility cannot stall the whole operation.

Losing a contract usually traces back to people and service fit, not price. Nemt Business Life, which built 100% self-pay up to 20 facility contracts, reports envious facility staff cutting trip volume or running 'patient not ready' games, resenting drivers who leave once the wait time expires, and sometimes pulling contracts outright [UtiLgcZo4dU @ 00:02:35]. The same operator lost a contract by taking last-minute trips, a direct contradiction of the always-available posture Marcus of All American Health teaches for building volume [UtiLgcZo4dU @ 00:14:00]. MJ Business Academy flags a service-level trap: ambulatory-only providers who chase hospice, which needs a gurney, or hospital discharges, which need wheelchair or gurney capability, will watch those callers 'eventually going to stop calling,' so the smarter target is same-day routine-surgery clinics [bX8mww6N5BM @ 00:07:33]. Duet NEMT names a quieter leak: posted website hours that start at 8:00 a.m. mean missing a lot of 5:00 a.m. dialysis runs, the very trips that recur multiple times a week and anchor a direct-pay book [caWAkt063_Q @ 00:00:46]. Every lost facility here traces back to saying yes to work the operation could not reliably cover, or to being unreachable when the work it could cover was available.

Unit economics punish broker-heavy and underpriced work. Nemiton puts broker-only businesses at 5 to 15% margins against 25 to 40% for operators diversified into direct facility and private pay, roughly triple the margin on the same vehicles [6nWzJ25nMDg @ 00:00:36]. Sherry C. Wright of Campton Transport lays out the broker math firsthand: paid in sevens, $14 for 7 miles and about $25 for 28 miles, with nothing paid for wait time [_BmJ_SxXCUY @ 00:50:38]. Mike Boron of Ambiance Medical Transportation bought a Los Angeles company running about 90% broker, declined its ambulatory line, and exited broker wheelchair work at $27 a ride, only to watch the brokers pull the gurney trips they had used as a reward for taking wheelchairs [bGYVSmlvo90 @ 00:01:47]. Boron still turns down health plans offering $110 per discharge because 'You cannot make money at 100,' a rate the operation treats as unprofitable on its face [bGYVSmlvo90 @ 00:14:41]. The check every operator should run before signing: does the per-trip number survive fuel, insurance, repairs, and a vehicle-replacement reserve, or is it volume that only keeps the vans moving while the balance sheet bleeds. Boron's answer was to stop chasing volume and price for the work itself.

callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, a lost contract, or a stalled ramp that a named operator lived through. Clear all four before adding a facility or a vehicle.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I set NEMT rates, bill trips, and hit my revenue targets?
chapters.title: NEMT Rates, Billing, and Unit Economics
chapters.subtitle: Rate formulas, rate sheets, rate structures, one-way billing, justifying rates, charging for deadhead miles, unpaid wait time, what Medicaid pays, how to bill trips, revenue lost to no-shows, startup costs, trips needed for $10K/month, and the $100K one-van, one-broker case
chapters.executive_summary: NEMT operators agree on four things. Brokers set most payouts. The broker-to-provider spread is where broker profit lives. The operator's own margin comes from trip selectivity, paid deadhead, priced wait time and a deliberate private pay book. ThatNEMTGirl grossed $125,000 in 2024 on one multi-load wheelchair van with one broker by refusing $35 filler trips. Shantasia_RN puts $10,000 of monthly revenue at roughly 200 trips averaging $50, with a floor of $500 per vehicle per week. The street mechanics are a base or load fee plus $2 to $5 per mile, $15 to $30 per 30 minutes of wait, radius-based deadhead charges and a monthly cost-per-mile check. Practitioners split on uniform versus tiered pricing, on whether to hand out rate sheets freely, and on how hard to chase broker volume versus private pay.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus - Brokers Set the Floor, Operators Build the Margin
paragraphs: Every speaker accepts that most volume arrives through a broker, and the broker pays on its own terms. RouteGenie states flatly that a majority of business will come from a broker that decides what it pays. That leaves room to negotiate only on special requests, such as trips outside your normal coverage zone [BuyVTPmpWAQ @ 00:00:22]. Nemt University describes the broker as the middleman sitting between Medicaid and your company. They name MTM, ModivCare (the former LogistiCare) and Access to Care as the main players, and say most states are broker states, with Michigan called out as an exception [ZerukPCXB6Q @ 00:08:36]. RouteGenie's sharpest point is about the spread. LogistiCare is paid on how many members it serves, while transportation companies are paid per trip performed, and that gap is where the broker's profit comes from [FBWU2kTGLwI @ 00:01:17]. The same video reports small companies opting out because the rates would not let them pay drivers more than minimum wage with no benefits. It answers the wait-time question with a blunt no: the broker does not pay for driver wait time at all. The leverage point is scarcity. If you are one of the only providers offering a certain service in your area, you can push for higher prices [FBWU2kTGLwI @ 00:00:59].

The second point of agreement is that pricing starts from your own cost structure, not a competitor's number. McKenzie of NEMT Growth Machine puts it as a rule: if your pricing is based on what the other guy charges instead of your actual cost structure, you do not own a business, you just have a job. For a one-to-three vehicle fleet, they name insurance or drivers as the number one cost, followed by vehicle payment and maintenance, website hosting and marketing [wens2SHO0_A @ 00:00:25]. The Nemt University hosts warn that operators budget for fuel and insurance but forget software subscriptions, marketing materials, depreciation and the value of their own time. They recommend breaking monthly overhead down into a per-day and even per-trip target [DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:02:04]. Shantasia, an RN who runs an NEMT company and a home care agency in North Carolina, makes the same point: revenue is not profit. Payroll, fuel, maintenance, insurance, taxes, software and office expenses come off the top, so focus on profit rather than gross [3tRytphhdUU @ 00:01:22]. RouteGenie adds that undercharging to attract customers can leave you unable to cover costs, and it drives down prices for the whole industry [OVN-rYxkYf8 @ 00:04:05].

Speakers also converge on trip selectivity and payer mix. ThatNEMTGirl tells operators they work with the broker, not for it, and do not have to take every trip offered. Their math: ten short ambulatory trips at $35 make $350 while burning gas and wear, but two $250 trips produce more profit with less work [govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:02:52]. They pair that with a rule for long-distance requests. A broker calling you for a trip one to two hours from home base is doing so because someone else cannot run it, so confirm the broker pays dead miles and, if it does, run it up [govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:04:44]. RouteGenie's billing video says private pay clients are less common but necessary to grow profitably. With private pay you set the rates yourself, including per-mile, deadhead miles and tolls, and you can collect cash, card or check as soon as the trip ends [EPbM9tmaF8E @ 00:01:52]. The Nemt University hosts follow the same payer-mix logic. They note the margin on a private pay client may be much higher than on a broker client, and they compare the service mix to a diversified investment portfolio [DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:02:35]. ThatNEMTGirl closes the loop by urging operators who are doing well with brokers to deliberately build up the private pay side of the portfolio [govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:05:31].

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers - The Rate Stack, Deadhead Math and the Quote
paragraphs: The rate stack the speakers teach is a load or base fee plus a per-mile charge, with surcharges layered on top. Nemt University's Medicaid video sets a base fee of $35 or $50 just to start the vehicle, plus $2 to $4 per mile. The speaker's own start fee is $40, while operators with higher costs might need $50 to $55. Wait time runs roughly $15 to $30 for 30 minutes [ZerukPCXB6Q @ 00:06:55]. RouteGenie's profitability chart runs wider: ambulatory base of $5 to $30 on weekdays; wheelchair base of $45 to $50 on weekdays and $75 to $90 on weekends and off hours; gurney base of $100 to $200 on weekdays; mileage of $3 to $5 per mile on weekdays, climbing to $5 to $10 on holidays; wait time of $15 to $30 per 30 minutes; and an additional attendant at $5 to $10 [qceSg9X8F0E @ 00:04:23]. The same channel describes three more pieces. A load fee covers the initial pickup. A minimum charge keeps a one- or two-mile trip from losing money. Flat rates negotiated with hospitals or nursing homes for frequent destinations give you a tool to land the account [BuyVTPmpWAQ @ 00:03:10]. It caps the stack with a market-reality warning: if the average wheelchair transport is $75, charging $150 for the same service puts you out of business [BuyVTPmpWAQ @ 00:01:52].

Deadhead math is where the speakers get most precise. In RouteGenie's ABC Transport example, a driver goes 40 miles out to pick up John Smith, so a two-leg trip is really four legs for the company. With a 25-mile service radius, the operator charges 15 deadhead miles each way, at a per-mile price of their choosing [9j6I5bSKP24 @ 00:02:19]. The one-way billing video runs a harder case. The service radius is 30 miles, the pickup is 20 miles east of the garage, and the drop-off is 60 miles west. That produces 80 total deadhead miles, a drop-off 30 miles beyond the footprint, nearly three hours of travel and roughly an hour with the vehicle out of region, and all of it must be priced in [wrfiCapUB9s @ 00:02:15]. To check whether those rates hold, the Nemt University hosts use the operating cost per mile formula: total monthly expenses divided by miles driven that month. They review it regularly as gas, competition and overhead shift [DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:05:12]. Nemt University's Medicaid video adds that when gas prices fluctuate, your price will likely have to fluctuate too [ZerukPCXB6Q @ 00:04:29]. Jasmine and Monica of MJ Business Academy report adding a surcharge when gas hit $7 to $8 a gallon [aA7hgZoPF_Q @ 00:02:16].

How the price reaches the customer matters as much as the number. McKenzie charges the base fee per leg, so a round trip pays it twice. They include no free miles and keep pricing simple enough that a caller can do quick mental math. For procedure patients who need a driver on site, The Doctor Ride drops the base and mileage fees and bills a flat hourly wait-and-return rate, priced differently for ambulatory and wheelchair [wens2SHO0_A @ 00:04:46]. After every quote call, they send the price by text and email. Their bet is that competitors rarely answer the phone, so a shopper coming back to book will call whoever gave them the price in writing [wens2SHO0_A @ 00:06:17]. The Nemt University hosts recommend quoting one flat total instead of itemizing every fee, and presenting the loading fee as a base rate so it does not read as an extra charge [DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:04:28]. MJ Business Academy says facilities will ask for your rate sheet first. If dispatch quotes rates off the top of their head, you are missing money. Their attendants carry a two-hour minimum booking. They also note that people hold onto old rate sheets for months or years, so state on the sheet that prices can vary [aA7hgZoPF_Q @ 00:10:21].

callout.title: Moves Operators Use to Squeeze More Out of Each Vehicle
callout.body: These are field tactics practitioners credit with raising revenue per van without simply adding more trips.
items: Buy a van that can carry two wheelchair clients at once, then multi-load riders going to nearby destinations, such as two dialysis patients around the corner from each other, instead of sending two vans [ThatNEMTGirl — govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:01:40].

Match operating hours to when brokers actually request trips. ThatNEMTGirl runs 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Monday through Friday and 6:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on Saturday [ThatNEMTGirl — govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:04:12].
Charge a premium for off-peak runs like a 4 a.m. dialysis transport, and frame it as a benefit: we are happy to accommodate those early morning hours [Nemt University — DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:09:42].

Add a second vehicle only when your broker portal or dispatch software shows trips going unclaimed that another driver could cover. Every new van also brings payroll, maintenance and insurance [Shantasia_RN — 3tRytphhdUU @ 00:02:08].

sop_steps.title: Build Your Cost-Per-Mile Baseline
sop_steps.action: Total every monthly expense and divide by the miles driven that month.
sop_steps.detail: Include insurance, drivers, vehicle payment, maintenance, hosting and marketing, then run the operating cost per mile formula and repeat it as gas and overhead change [Nemt University — DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:05:12] [NEMT Growth Machine — wens2SHO0_A @ 00:00:51].

sop_steps.title: Call Around and Map the Local Market
sop_steps.action: Call competitors posing as a family member and request quotes for a sample trip.
sop_steps.detail: Ask what a ride from here to there costs. Note what each company actually includes, not just the price, so you can set a rough range for your own rates [NEMT Growth Machine — wens2SHO0_A @ 00:02:30].

sop_steps.title: Set the Rate Stack and Deadhead Radius
sop_steps.action: Define a load fee, per-mile rate, minimum charge, surcharges and a service radius.
sop_steps.detail: Bill deadhead miles for anything beyond the radius, as in the 25-mile radius example that yields 15 billed miles each way. Layer holiday, weekend and after-hours rates on top [RouteGenie — 9j6I5bSKP24 @ 00:02:19] [RouteGenie — OVN-rYxkYf8 @ 00:07:38].

sop_steps.title: Publish the Rate Sheet and Lock Every Quote
sop_steps.action: Hand facilities a branded rate sheet, verify coverage before each trip, and send written quotes.
sop_steps.detail: Facilities will ask for the rate sheet first. Before the trip, confirm whether the rider is Medicaid or private pay and verify name, date of birth, address and phone [MJ Business Academy — aA7hgZoPF_Q @ 00:03:26] [RouteGenie — EPbM9tmaF8E @ 00:02:38].

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is where the money comes from. ThatNEMTGirl ran one rear-entry manual-ramp van on a single broker contract and reports it did $125,000, built on multi-loading wheelchair riders and weeding out low-dollar work, with the line 'you do not work for the broker, you work with the broker' [govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:01:22]. RouteGenie frames the opposite reality: most business arrives through a broker, and the broker decides what it pays, leaving negotiation only for special requests such as trips outside your normal coverage zone [BuyVTPmpWAQ @ 00:00:22]. McKenzie of NEMT Growth Machine went the other direction from day one, telling viewers that with one vehicle the team deliberately aimed at private pay instead of the broker model, and priced for a premium audience that wants a consistently clean, on-time van rather than the cheapest ride [wens2SHO0_A @ 00:01:31]. The Nemt University podcast hosts land in the middle, arguing that private-pay margin can be much higher than broker margin, so an operator should map ideal income, required trip count, and which channel those trips come from, treating the mix like a diversified portfolio [DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:02:35]. The practical read: broker-only operators win on loading density and trip selection, while private-pay operators win on rate control and must market harder to fill the van.

Practitioners also clash on how a rate gets built. McKenzie's rule is blunt: if your pricing is based on what the other guy charges instead of your actual cost structure, you don't own a business, you just have a job [wens2SHO0_A @ 00:00:25]. RouteGenie pushes back from the market side, warning that if the average wheelchair transport in your area is $75, you will go out of business charging $150 for the same service, unless you offer a specialized service nobody else runs, which gives leverage for higher prices [BuyVTPmpWAQ @ 00:01:52]. On rate-sheet count, the Nemt University hosts report that the owners they interviewed favor one uniform price whenever contracts allow, because fewer rate sheets are easier to manage, yet later in the same episode they call a one-size-fits-all rate a common mistake when you juggle private pay, broker contracts, and facility partnerships [DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:05:54]. Presentation splits too: the podcast says hand the client one flat total amount with no itemized receipt, arguing it prevents awkward moments where a client questions a specific charge, while RouteGenie's rate-justification playbook tells operators to break down load fee, minimum charge, per-mile, and after-hours surcharges so passengers see exactly what they pay for [OVN-rYxkYf8 @ 00:07:22].

Wait time is where fee schedules diverge most. Nemt University quotes a rule of thumb of $15 to $30 per 30 minutes of waiting, framing it as making sure your time is accounted for because your time is valuable [ZerukPCXB6Q @ 00:12:36]. McKenzie rejects time-slice billing on the per-leg product, arguing that charging every 15 minutes or handing out free miles kills the caller's ability to do quick mental math; instead The Doctor Ride charges a base fee per leg with zero free miles, then runs a separate wait-and-return service that wipes the base and mileage fees and bills a flat hourly rate, priced differently for ambulatory and wheelchair, and marketed on the website because many local competitors do not offer to wait [wens2SHO0_A @ 00:05:27]. MJ Business Academy's Jasmine and Monica sell attendant time with a hard floor, a two-hour minimum on attendant bookings, and insist wait time be printed on the rate sheet because facilities ask whether the vehicle can stay idle [aA7hgZoPF_Q @ 00:07:07]. Booking channels split as well: Jasmine and Monica say embedding self-scheduling on your website means you are missing money because questions need to happen between scheduling, while RouteGenie pushes passenger portals and apps for schedule customization to cut no-shows [eKdj-HOLoXU @ 00:05:00].
