sections.heading: 4. Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The broker rate is the first trap operators hit. RouteGenie states flatly that LogistiCare, now Modivcare, does not pay providers for driver wait time at all, and that many small companies opt out because the rates would not let them pay drivers more than minimum wage with no benefits; the broker is paid per member served while providers are paid per trip performed, and that gap is where the broker's profit sits [FBWU2kTGLwI @ 00:00:41]. The one lever named is scarcity: if you are one of the only companies in your area providing a certain service, you have room to negotiate higher prices [FBWU2kTGLwI @ 00:00:59]. ThatNEMTGirl puts the volume trap in numbers: ten short ambulatory trips at $35 gross only $350 for the day while burning gas and wear and tear, whereas two $250 payouts beat that with less work [govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:02:52]. The same operator warns that long-distance broker calls, an hour to two hours from home base, usually exist because somebody else could not do them, so confirm the broker pays dead miles before accepting, and only then run it up [govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:04:44]. Treat any broker trip that ignores wait and dead miles as a cost line, not revenue.

Revenue claims are the second trap. Shantasia_RN, a registered nurse running NEMT in North Carolina, does the arithmetic: at an average $50 per completed trip, $10,000 in monthly revenue takes roughly 200 completed trips, and that is revenue, not profit, before payroll, fuel, maintenance, insurance, taxes, software, and office costs [3tRytphhdUU @ 00:01:00]. The same operator admits assuming a second vehicle automatically meant more money, then learning it meant another driver, more payroll, more maintenance, more insurance, and more headaches; the fix is to add a vehicle only when unclaimed trips are sitting in the broker portal, and to check first because brokers are now requiring new providers to have more than one vehicle [3tRytphhdUU @ 00:01:44]. In a separate clip Shantasia sets a floor of $500 per week per vehicle across a five-vehicle fleet, totaling $2,500 per week as the minimum, and declines to share actual numbers [Dr_9wzpyoaE @ 00:00:15], while RouteGenie pegs average owner earnings at $40,000 to $60,000 a year, noting the longer owners stay in business the more they earn as regular customers build up [qceSg9X8F0E @ 00:03:45]. Plan the second van off proven unfilled demand, not off the headline number.

The last set of traps are operational leaks. RouteGenie cites a study where 46 percent of scheduled appointments were canceled by patients, says more than 67 percent of no-show patients simply did not understand how to cancel or reschedule, and recommends a written no-show policy, often a 24-hour free-cancellation window, agreed before the first booking [eKdj-HOLoXU @ 00:01:06]. One of the MJ Business Academy hosts admits to avoiding sending out the rate sheet because facilities hold onto it six months to two years and expect those prices honored, so any shared sheet must state that prices vary, a lesson learned when gas hit $7 to $8 a gallon and a surcharge went on; worse, a dispatcher quoting rates off the top of the head is missing money [aA7hgZoPF_Q @ 00:01:53]. The Nemt University hosts name undervaluing as the most common mistake, a race to the bottom driven by forgetting depreciation, marketing, and owner time, and prescribe the operating cost per mile formula: total monthly expenses divided by miles driven that month [DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:08:24]. RouteGenie adds that one out-of-footprint one-way order can stack 80 deadhead miles and nearly three hours of travel, and charging the same rate for all trips hits profitability through losses or reduced margin on after-hours work [wrfiCapUB9s @ 00:02:15].

callout.title: Four Checks Before You Commit a Van, a Contract, or a Quote
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, leak, or reversal the practitioners hit themselves. Clear all four before taking on new volume.
items: Before accepting a long-distance broker trip an hour or more from home base, confirm the broker pays dead miles; if it does, run it up [ThatNEMTGirl — govQRXzu6Rg @ 00:04:44].
Do not buy another vehicle until extra unclaimed trips are visible in the broker portal or dispatch software [Shantasia_RN — 3tRytphhdUU @ 00:02:08].
Run the operating cost per mile formula, total monthly expenses divided by monthly miles, and reprice when rates stop covering it [Nemt University — DoH4BLPOrvI @ 00:05:12].
Every rate sheet sent to a facility states prices can vary over time, so a surcharge like the $7 to $8 gas spike can be added [MJ Business Academy — aA7hgZoPF_Q @ 00:02:16].

chapters.question_prompt: What dispatch software and trip-verification systems do I need to run efficiently and survive audits and fraud crackdowns?
chapters.title: Dispatch Software, Trip Verification, and Fraud Enforcement
chapters.subtitle: How NEMT dispatch systems work, RouteGenie, Bambi, MediRoutes, and MediRydes walkthroughs, multi-load setup, software demos, Modivcare app trip booking, GPS tracking, proving every trip in tightening audits, overcoming fraud, $12M fake-ride and GPS spoofing cases, Congress's trip-verification bill, and broker accountability in New Jersey
chapters.executive_summary: NEMT software vendors, operators, and enforcement reporting converge on one rule: a trip that cannot be proven will not get paid and may get prosecuted. RouteGenie tracks HR 10618's proposed six-point electronic verification and a DOJ case over $12 million in allegedly fraudulent rides built on GPS-spoofed coordinates, while WTEN shows an operator charged after already settling for $1.1 million. Street mechanics center on bulk auto-dispatch (Bambi solving 41 trips in about 10 seconds, MediRoutes assigning 100 daily trips in under 60 seconds), in-app timestamps, signatures, breadcrumbs, geofences, dash cams, and claim scrubbing that SwiftAid credits with cutting denials from 23% to 6%. Disagreement centers on pricing and usability: Bambi's flat per-car pricing versus RouteGenie's $50 base plus setup, messaging, and $250 training fees, and ZeitRide's $50 small-fleet play.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: Proof of Trip Is Now the Product
paragraphs: Every vendor and operator in this lane lands on the same baseline: if you cannot prove the trip, you will not keep the money. MediRydes states flatly that many brokers require NEMT providers to run dispatch software at all [6lnCunvrFc4 @ 00:00:25], and the NEMT host on the ZeitRide episode, seven years in the business, says the email-and-text era is over because an emailed work order collapses into he-said, she-said the moment an auditor shows up [ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:02:54]. RouteGenie's October recap frames HR 10618, the Stop Medicaid Fraud Act, as a proposal that would push electronic verification on every state from January 1st, 2027, keyed to six data points: service, recipient, provider, date, location, and start and end time [_mEgB7bAsFE @ 00:00:38]. Their read is that a GPS-equipped dispatch system already records all six on every trip, and broker contracts have demanded them for years. The SwiftAid deep dive puts the stakes in dollars: a 2022 Inspector General audit of New York found $196 million in improper payments with 72% of audited claims non-compliant [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:03:28]. The consensus is blunt. Documentation is no longer back-office hygiene; it is the asset brokers, payers, and auditors are actually buying.

Practitioners also agree that raw GPS is necessary but not sufficient. RouteGenie's August recap walks through the DOJ racketeering case against four alleged members of the so-called war room, tied to more than $12 million in allegedly fraudulent Medicaid transportation claims. The detail that matters most: the war room was not a transport company but an outside shop that logged trips that never happened and used a GPS spoofing application to fake pickup and drop-off coordinates, then supplied the data to companies that billed Medicaid [GWBpqyUYyjE @ 00:01:43]. The claims surfaced as unmatched, meaning no medical provider ever billed a corresponding visit, which is why RouteGenie says strong records must tie location to passenger, appointment, timestamps, driver activity, credentials, and billing so the data tells one consistent story [GWBpqyUYyjE @ 00:02:52]. WTEN's coverage of Angel Medical Transportation shows the enforcement loop does not stop at a settlement: after a $1.1 million deal, the Schenectady DA says the owner was still in business doing the same stuff, now charged over an alleged $1.8 million scheme [qMb3ANIPN3Y @ 00:00:42]. The SwiftAid breakdown names the two patterns auditors hunt, ghost trips and mileage inflation, where a legitimate 10-mile run gets written up as 20 [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:04:35].

The third point of agreement is that the same software stack that proves trips also protects margin by killing no-shows and wasted dispatches. RouteGenie claims its en-route reminder calls plus passenger app tracking cut no-show rates up to 50% [j__fVq5xHLo @ 00:01:37], while the SwiftAid deep dive cites a New York provider whose live SMS tracking link dropped inbound where's-my-ride calls by 60% and an industry no-show rate falling from about 30% to under 10% [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:15:02]. The rider side explains why this matters: JerseyTogether riders describe being told to book an hour early to compensate for late drivers, waiting three and a half hours as Ubers got dispatched one after another, and one rider hitchhiking on Route 10 after no return pickup came [2H1uLI5MuZo @ 00:01:14]. Operators who cannot show on-time and completed-trip data inherit that reputation, and RouteGenie argues that completed-trip and on-time rates are now the language health plans are measured in, backed by a Mayo Clinic study showing patients with unmet transportation needs were 5.2 percentage points less likely to show up [_mEgB7bAsFE @ 00:04:11]. The shared takeaway: reminders and live tracking are revenue tools, not courtesy features.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the dispatch floor, the mechanic every vendor demos is bulk auto-assignment. In the Bambi demo, the dispatcher loads 41 trips against six driver shifts, selects all, and hits Run Bambi Run; in roughly 10 seconds it returns a suggestion screen with blue new assignments and purple reassignments that move trips between drivers to cut total fleet drive time [CbCgWxHPCxU @ 00:02:16]. The Nemt University walkthrough shows the same engine weighing pickup and drop-off locations, historic traffic, bariatric wheelchair needs, and driver skills, then leaving stretcher trips unassigned when the stretcher van starts too late to make a 7:30 pickup [mgK4ir9UXtc @ 00:03:24]. MediRoutes' fictional A1 NEMT example runs 100 trips a day across about seven vehicles, importing LogistiCare and MTM files, calculating pickup times from load, drive, and unload time, enforcing a contract rule that school kids never ride with adults, and finishing assignment in under 60 seconds with a revenue-per-mile readout for every vehicle before anyone leaves the yard [nLjDVheWODU @ 00:02:41]. RouteGenie claims its pre-routing fits up to 20% more trips on the same vehicles and drivers and lifts routing and dispatch efficiency by as much as 25% [j__fVq5xHLo @ 00:01:20].

Trip proof is built from timestamps the driver cannot backfill after the fact. In the MediRoutes flow, driver Steve performs a pull-out that stamps payroll time, marks arrival, then performs the pickup on departure so dispatch knows the exact passenger wait, and the app prompts an electronic signature at drop-off that transmits immediately [nLjDVheWODU @ 00:04:53]. The SwiftAid deep dive layers on breadcrumb logging, a GPS coordinate and timestamp dropped every few seconds, plus dispatcher-drawn geofences around a dialysis center or a patient's block that log the exact moment the van enters and exits without the driver tapping anything [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:07:45]. That feeds the triple match: broker or doctor authorization, GPS performance, and an invoice whose mileage matches the breadcrumbs; if one key is off, the claim is denied [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:08:34]. The host on the ZeitRide episode reports auditors now check whether driver photos match what is on Google Maps, while ZeitRide's Amanda says the company can supply a dash cam and cut footage into clips from the second of pickup [ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:28:29]. ZeitRide pitches the payoff as producing a full audit package in 10 minutes instead of a week of scrambling.

Software pricing is where operators get the sharpest numbers. A buyer on the Bambi podcast, standing up a two-to-three car transport arm, itemized RouteGenie's pricing as $50 per vehicle per month plus a $100 setup fee, 2.5 cents per reminder text, 5 cents per reminder call, and $250 for a one-hour one-on-one training session, against Bambi's flat 67 dollars per car [CbCgWxHPCxU @ 00:09:57]. The same buyer contrasted those add-ons with a single per-car Bambi price the founder called set in stone and listed on the website, with no extra charge for support sessions. The SwiftAid deep dive lists Bambi starting around $69 per vehicle per month [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:21:38], while ZeitRide quotes about $50 a month per vehicle and frames it as roughly the revenue of one ride, with the host calling $50 per vehicle very competitive [ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:22:24]. The payback math in the SwiftAid breakdown is aggressive: a Texas provider saving over $50,000 on fuel in six months and absorbing 25% more monthly trips without new vehicles or drivers, and Metro Medical Transport cutting claim denials from 23% to 6% to recover an extra $200,000 a month [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:37:06].

callout.title: Dispatch-Floor Edges Operators Are Already Using
callout.body: These are the specific moves practitioners call out for capturing more trips, filling capacity gaps, and walking into rate conversations with numbers.
items: Turn facilities into a captive order channel: give a nurse or transport coordinator a facility-user login so they add trips and track only their own patients; one customer's facilities stopped ordering from the competing NEMT business and sent more trips than the fleet could cover [Nemt University — mgK4ir9UXtc @ 00:07:27].

Enable multi-loading payer by payer before trying to build a manual multi-load, then set pickup and drop-off order explicitly so the driver app shows the right sequence [Bambi — dxaejS8Bpis @ 00:00:15].

Push ambulatory overflow to rideshare from inside dispatch: RouteGenie now assigns appropriate trips to Uber Health in the existing workflow, with Uber statuses and trip IDs mapping back into trip details [RouteGenie — GWBpqyUYyjE @ 00:08:20].

Bring Minnesota's fuel-indexed formula into rate talks: wheelchair mileage moved to $1.92 per loaded mile from $1.76 and stretcher to $2.71 from $2.49, adjusting with fuel prices every quarter [RouteGenie — _mEgB7bAsFE @ 00:04:53].

sop_steps.title: Lock the intake pipeline
sop_steps.action: Pull broker trips through import or API instead of retyping them
sop_steps.detail: Double data entry is called the primary cause of death for Medicaid claims; one transposed digit in a Medicaid ID gets a flawlessly driven trip denied, so let the software pull the broker payload directly [SwiftAid Transport — YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:28:29].

sop_steps.title: Auto-route, then sanity-check
sop_steps.action: Run bulk assignment across the full day and review what stays unassigned
sop_steps.detail: Run the optimizer, accept or override suggestions, and treat unassigned stretcher or bariatric trips as a capacity signal rather than sending a vehicle that cannot do the job [Nemt University — mgK4ir9UXtc @ 00:03:24].

sop_steps.action: Require in-app pull-out, arrival, pickup, drop-off, and signature on every trip
sop_steps.detail: Pull-out creates the payroll timestamp, arrival and pickup create the wait-time record, and the drop-off signature transmits immediately, eliminating paper logs [MediRoutes NEMT Software — nLjDVheWODU @ 00:04:39].

sop_steps.title: Build the audit packet before the audit
sop_steps.action: Bundle GPS, timestamps, signatures, photos, and billing per trip
sop_steps.detail: A 30-day audit with no proof can leave a provider missing $12,000 to $15,000; the ZeitRide episode host has been audited and could prove some trips but not those run without software or cameras [ZeitRide NEMT Software — ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:29:51].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is over how dispatch software should be bought and what it really costs. A transportation lead evaluating platforms for a new two-to-three car fleet walked out of a RouteGenie demo and itemized the stack: $50 per month per vehicle, a $100 setup fee, 2.5 cents per reminder text, 5 cents per reminder call, and $250 for one hour of one-on-one training, against Bambi's flat 67 dollars per car with nothing bolted on [CbCgWxHPCxU @ 00:09:17]. RouteGenie's own pitch takes the opposite posture, bundling up to eight training sessions with an implementation specialist, phone and email support through the day, optional on-site launch support, and paid customization where time and cost vary per request [j__fVq5xHLo @ 00:02:25]. ZeitRide holds at about $50 a month per vehicle and frames it as roughly the cost of a single ride, while the episode host calls that price very competitive and notes the real decision is per-vehicle versus per-volume billing [ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:22:24]. SwiftAid Transport's market survey places Bambi around $69 a month per vehicle for small fleets without an IT department and reserves RouteGenie for the 40-to-50 van mid-market, where broker synchronization matters more than interface polish [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:21:38]. The operator move is to price the entire fee schedule, not the headline seat rate.

Practitioners also split on what a dispatcher should actually be staring at all day. Bambi's team tells operators they really do not need the live map, because the color-coded trip boxes on the dispatch calendar expand, contract, and change status in real time as drivers tap through the driver app, giving a living view of the whole fleet at once [mgK4ir9UXtc @ 00:05:04]. RouteGenie argues the reverse priority: seeing every vehicle in real time is what lets a dispatcher redirect a driver mid-route around traffic and road conditions before a late arrival happens [382JPpV04Tg @ 00:02:13]. MediRoutes sits between the two camps, pairing a dashboard of every vehicle's location and trip status with a real-time will-call engine that recommends the best driver by space type, vehicle capacity, proximity, and riders already on board [nLjDVheWODU @ 00:05:40]. On optimization, everyone agrees automation beats hand-assignment, but they disagree on how far to trust it. Run Bambi Run drafts a full day in under 30 seconds and leaves stretcher trips visibly unassigned when capacity does not exist, yet Bambi's own knowledge base still has dispatchers build multi-loads by hand, enabling multi-loading separately for each payer and manually setting the pickup and drop-off order [dxaejS8Bpis @ 00:00:30]. The working playbook: let the optimizer draft the day, then hand-correct multi-loads and exceptions before applying.

The deepest split is over what actually counts as proof of a trip. RouteGenie's August news desk says GPS is still essential, but coordinates on their own are not the whole picture: a strong record ties location data to passenger information, appointments, timestamps, driver activity, credentials, and billing, and the bar is moving from collecting data to showing that the data tells one consistent story [GWBpqyUYyjE @ 00:02:34]. SwiftAid Transport turns that into a triple match, comparing an audit to a vault that needs three keys turned together: the broker or doctor authorization, the GPS breadcrumb and geofence trigger proving the route, and an invoice whose mileage matches the breadcrumbs, with any mismatch leaving the claim denied [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:08:16]. The ZeitRide episode argues auditors already want more than pings, describing reviewers pulling driver photos and checking whether they match Google Maps imagery, with ZeitRide offering a dash cam whose footage can be cut into clips from the second of pickup [ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:28:29]. RouteGenie's fraud guide reaches the same hardware answer from the other direction, telling operators to consider in-vehicle cameras to prevent trips run with an empty vehicle when a driver is partnering with a passenger [VSyBnPDVpR8 @ 00:07:25]. GPS-only operators sit at the weakest end of that spectrum.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure practitioners describe is not fraud; it is honest work that cannot be proven. The host of the ZeitRide episode, a seven-year operator, says flatly they have been the provider under audit: some trips proved out, others had no software and no cameras behind them, and a single 30-day audit window can leave an operator missing $12,000 to $15,000 for a month of unprovable trips [ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:29:32]. The same host walks through a recent dispute where a client rode to an appointment the doctor's office had tried to cancel by phone, the insurer pushed back on paying the two legs, and the only question left on the table was where is the proof [ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:08:57]. SwiftAid Transport scales that exposure up: a 2022 New York audit uncovered $196 million in improper payments, with 72 percent of audited claims found non-compliant, which the hosts read as a structural feature of a paper-based industry rather than a few bad apples [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:03:28]. RouteGenie flags where the bar is heading, with HR 10618 proposing electronic verification on six data points per trip, covering service, recipient, provider, date, location, and start and end time, from January 1, 2027, while stressing it is a proposal, not law [_mEgB7bAsFE @ 00:01:00]. Email threads and paper logs do not clear that standard.

Enforcement stories show how fast a billing shortcut becomes a criminal case. WTEN reports Angel Medical Transportation was one of 25 New York transportation companies accused of Medicaid fraud by the attorney general, reached a $1.1 million settlement, and, in the Schenectady County District Attorney's words, was still in business, still doing the same stuff [qMb3ANIPN3Y @ 00:00:42]. The new charges allege a scheme topping $1.8 million built on ride claims that never happened, overbilled group rides, lied-about destinations used to inflate payments, and kickbacks paid to Medicaid recipients by the office manager [qMb3ANIPN3Y @ 00:01:10]. RouteGenie's August recap covers the DOJ racketeering case against the so-called war room, an outside operation that allegedly manufactured ride data and used a GPS spoofing application to falsify pickup and drop-off coordinates, then supplied it to companies that billed Medicaid; the claims surfaced as unmatched because no medical provider ever billed a corresponding visit, and the defendants are presumed innocent [GWBpqyUYyjE @ 00:01:43]. SwiftAid Transport stacks the per-claim math on top: False Claims Act penalties of $14,000 to $29,000 per false claim plus triple damages, meaning 50 ghost trips slipped in by a rogue driver can approach a million dollars in fines for an owner who never knew [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:05:21]. Bought or borrowed trip data is a business-ending liability.

The daily traps are smaller but they compound fast. ZeitRide's Amanda and the episode host both flag the mismatched-vehicle cancel: a driver shows up without the ramp, width, or length a bariatric wheelchair client needs because someone missed the notes, the trip gets cancelled, and the revenue disappears along with the client's day [ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:16:23]. SwiftAid Transport traces most billing losses to double data entry, where a dispatcher retyping a broker trip transposes two digits of a Medicaid ID and a flawless ride gets denied; Metro Medical Transport ran a 23 percent manual denial rate, essentially working nearly a quarter of its trips for free, until automated scrubbing and API imports cut it to 6 percent in six months [YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:37:06]. Broker-side failures land directly on riders: New Jersey Medicaid members describe padding every appointment by an hour just to arrive on time, getting stranded for hours, and in one case a doctor refusing to see a patient who arrived late [2H1uLI5MuZo @ 00:00:20]. Even the Modivcare booking flow carries a built-in denial trigger, warning that selecting a companion when the member's benefit plan does not allow one means the ride may be denied, and that height and weight entries drive which vehicle is sent [B7gusCVjbQY @ 00:02:45].

callout.title: Trip-Proof Gate Before Any Claim or Contract Moves
callout.body: Four pass/fail checks built from losses, denials, and enforcement cases practitioners reported firsthand. Fail any one and the trip does not bill or the contract does not start.
items: Enroll and credential with any incoming broker before the transition date; Montana Medicaid trips require Modivcare enrollment, and late enrollees wait on paperwork while others carry day-one trips [RouteGenie — GWBpqyUYyjE @ 00:06:24].
Hold any trip that does not carry all six verification points: service, recipient, provider, date, location, and start and end time [RouteGenie — _mEgB7bAsFE @ 00:01:00].
Block any claim where GPS breadcrumb mileage does not match the invoiced mileage; one jagged key in the triple match keeps the claim denied [SwiftAid Transport — YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:08:34].
Prove you can pull a full audit packet of signatures, timestamps, routes, and photos in about 10 minutes instead of a week of scrambling [ZeitRide NEMT Software — ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:22:43].

chapters.pull_quote: "They will come through with not just one trip, not just two trips, a whole 30 days worth of audits ... and next thing you know you're missing $12,000, $15,000." — ZeitRide NEMT Software (ajqkD-2jPd8 @ 00:29:32).
action_checklist: Pipe broker trips straight into dispatch through imports or API so nobody retypes Medicaid IDs, since one transposed digit gets a flawless ride denied [SwiftAid Transport — YGC_f04Hg3g @ 00:28:44].

Require driver-app timestamps for pull-out, arrival, pickup, and drop-off, and capture passenger or facility e-signatures in the app to retire paper logs [MediRoutes NEMT Software — nLjDVheWODU @ 00:04:39].
Send automated reminders the day before, the day of, and when the driver departs, letting passengers cancel before the dry run [RouteGenie — V_r1oFY0--w @ 00:01:42].
Give facility coordinators partial logins limited to adding trip requests, viewing only their facility's trips, and tracking them live on the map [Bambi — CbCgWxHPCxU @ 00:14:21].
Train drivers to confirm drop-off at the booked facility and add in-vehicle cameras to shut down empty-vehicle ghost rides [RouteGenie — VSyBnPDVpR8 @ 00:07:09].
Run a quarterly audit drill: export invoices by date range and payer to a QuickBooks-format CSV and match each to its trip proof [Bambi — CbCgWxHPCxU @ 00:21:08].
